summary: Informal podcast-style customer interview focusing on Acme Analytics' experience with Redwood Inference: migration from managed endpoints, cost and latency wins, security/compliance needs, and a request to produce a case study and quote for marketing assets.
transcript:
[00:00:00] Alex Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. This is Alex from Redwood, and with me is Sofia, our product marketing manager. We're recording a short customer conversation for a marketing piece — casual — feel free to be candid.
[00:00:18] Jordan Lee: Hi Alex, hi Sofia. Thanks for having us. Jordan here, Head of Marketing at Acme Analytics. We're excited to share our story.
[00:00:28] Cam Nguyen: Cam — VP Product. I'll jump in on the technical bits.
[00:00:33] Taylor Brooks: Taylor from CS, quick note: I'll help with any logistics around approvals.
[00:00:42] Alex Morgan: Great. Quick opener — could you tell us a bit about Acme's product and how you're using LLMs today? Keep it high level, like who you're serving and the user problem.
[00:00:55] Jordan Lee: Sure. So Acme builds analytics pipelines for retail chains, right. Our customers want conversational reporting — they want to ask questions like, why did sales dip in aisle five last week — and get a narrative plus suggested actions. We started with a small prototype using a third-party API, and as usage grew it became clear we needed predictable latency and better cost control.
[00:01:18] Cam Nguyen: Yeah, the prototype used a hosted model, um, and we saw pretty variable latency during peak times — which broke our SLAs for certain customers. So we engaged Redwood for inference serving.
[00:01:30] Alex Morgan: Nice. Can you quantify the impact — latency improvements, cost per 1k tokens, anything you can share?
[00:01:40] Cam Nguyen: We can share ballpark numbers. After moving the core generation paths to Redwood Dedicated and enabling prefix caching, our p50 latency for the main prompt dropped from ~420ms to ~180ms, and p95 dropped from nearly 1.8s to about 600-700ms. Cost-wise, per-token cost went down roughly 30% once we tuned batching and moved to a quantized model variant.
[00:02:04] Jordan Lee: And from a business POV that meant we could offer a new SLA tier for enterprise customers. We saw churn decrease in those accounts because responses felt snappier.
[00:02:15] Sofia Reyes: That's great — when you say quantized model variant, did Redwood help with recommendations there?
[00:02:21] Cam Nguyen: Yeah, the Redwood team did a model profile and suggested a 4-bit quantized variant for our workload, which kept output quality within our eval thresholds. There was a bit of a tradeoff, like slight change in temperature retention on some prompts, but overall it was within acceptable boundaries.
[00:02:38] Alex Morgan: Were there any surprises during the migration? Anything that caused delays or needed special workarounds?
[00:02:44] Cam Nguyen: A couple. Our internal infra uses strict VPC peering and we have an HSM for key management. The initial Private deployment required some networking tweaks — nothing huge but the routing and egress rules needed a careful pass. Also, we had to coordinate SSO and RBAC mapping to match our org structure.
[00:03:02] Taylor Brooks: Right, and for audit purposes we asked for longer retention on request logs for a subset of clients. Redwood's console had support for exporting traces and token-level cost data which made our compliance review easier, but we did have a question about encryption at rest and KMS integration.
[00:03:18] Cam Nguyen: On that, Redwood integrated with our KMS and provided an audit trail; they also provided SOC 2 docs which helped the security team sign off. The only mis-step was a mislabel in the initial audit doc — small typo — but it was corrected quickly.
[00:03:33] Jordan Lee: The security review was a gating factor for us — we couldn't move forward with certain enterprise customers without it. The Redwood team were pretty responsive which gave us confidence.
[00:03:42] Sofia Reyes: How did your product teams like the SDKs and dev experience?
[00:03:47] Cam Nguyen: SDKs were straightforward. We did hit one weird bug with streaming responses where the client library mis-attributed speaker labels — honestly that was more on our integration and it took a short hotfix. The realtime streaming worked after enabling a couple of flags.
[00:04:03] Alex Morgan: Do you still use hosted API for any workloads?
[00:04:07] Cam Nguyen: Yes — we kept the hosted API for lightweight, low-stakes internal tools and monitoring jobs. For customer-facing inference we moved traffic to Dedicated and Private as we needed the isolation and SLOs.
[00:04:19] Jordan Lee: And in marketing we highlight that we use a dedicated infra for our enterprise customers, because that maps to the trust signals our buyers expect.
[00:04:28] Alex Morgan: Love that. For the case study, we're planning to highlight the business metrics and a short quote. Would you be comfortable with a short written quote from you Jordan and a headshot?
[00:04:37] Jordan Lee: Yeah, happy to do that. We'll get a couple of options.
[00:04:41] Taylor Brooks: I'll coordinate the approvals and make sure the legal folks are looped in if needed.
[00:04:47] Sofia Reyes: Thank you. A couple of storytelling questions: can you share a specific customer scenario or anecdote where the latency improved outcomes?
[00:04:57] Jordan Lee: Sure. One retailer used the conversational insights during a store manager briefing. Previously they received a long batch report the next day. With our near-real-time narrative, the store manager asked follow-ups live and implemented a price change that afternoon — the next week they saw a measurable uptick in conversion.
[00:05:18] Cam Nguyen: Another example: our anomaly detector surfaces candidate explanations, and with lower latency we could run a deeper reranking step without breaking UX time budgets. That saved an extra engineering pipeline we had previously queued.
[00:05:31] Alex Morgan: Any metrics on conversion lift or revenue impact?
[00:05:35] Jordan Lee: We can attribute about a 3-5% lift for stores that used the realtime recommendations and an +8% on promotional uplifts when managers acted on the insights the same day. It's early data but promising.
[00:05:48] Sofia Reyes: Excellent. Let's pivot briefly to adoption and rollout — how did you enable customers to migrate, any docs or onboarding best practices?
[00:05:56] Taylor Brooks: We created a migration playbook and an onboarding checklist. We also offered a 6-week pilot where we set up the Dedicated instance, ran a set of benchmark prompts, and validated quality with our eval harness. That pilot helped de-risk the move.
[00:06:12] Cam Nguyen: The eval harness used an automated prompt set and human-in-the-loop checks for edge cases. Redwood's Optimize recommendations were useful here — they suggested caching policies and batching thresholds.
[00:06:25] Alex Morgan: You mentioned audit logs earlier — were there specific compliance requests from customers that influenced how you configured retention and logging?
[00:06:34] Jordan Lee: Yes, some buyers in EU requested data residency and extended retention for logs for audit reasons. We set up region-locked deployments and longer log retention for those clients. Redwood supported region routing which made this less painful.
[00:06:47] Cam Nguyen: There was a bit of confusion early about what data Redwood stores by default — we had to clarify which artifacts were persisted and for how long. That was in the security FAQ we co-produced.
[00:06:58] Alex Morgan: Sounds like a good partnership. Any feature asks or roadmap items you wish Redwood had prioritized earlier?
[00:07:06] Cam Nguyen: From a product point of view, better first-party evaluation tools in the console would be nice — like an integrated prompt regression dashboard. Redwood has some of that, but a few more out-of-the-box comparisons would save time.
[00:07:19] Jordan Lee: Also, more granular RBAC templates for marketing vs product roles would help speed internal approvals.
[00:07:26] Sofia Reyes: Good feedback — we'll bring that to the product team.
[00:07:30] Alex Morgan: Switching gears— we sometimes hear concerns about hallucinations or model regressions after quantization. Did you see any customer-facing quality issues?
[00:07:39] Cam Nguyen: A couple minor regressions on entity-name handling in some edge prompts; we rolled back a config and adjusted the sampling settings — that fixed it. The Redwood eval alerts helped catch some of these regressions during canary rollouts.
[00:07:53] Jordan Lee: The ability to pin model versions per route was crucial — we couldn't risk silent changes rolling into production.
[00:07:59] Alex Morgan: Great. For the marketing asset, we're also thinking of a short 10-15 minute podcast-style clip with highlights. Would you be open to recording a short extract we could publicly post?
[00:08:10] Jordan Lee: Yeah, Jordan here — I'm comfortable. We're just conscious about not divulging customer PII or specific contract numbers.
[00:08:18] Taylor Brooks: We'll approve any quotes. We prefer to sign off on the final script.
[00:08:23] Sofia Reyes: Totally understandable — we'll send the transcript first for approvals.
[00:08:27] Alex Morgan: Perfect. One last operational question — any notes on billing or pricing that affected how you positioned the value to customers?
[00:08:36] Jordan Lee: The predictability of Dedicated pricing allowed us to design fixed-price tiers for enterprise customers. That changed our go-to-market messaging because we could promise performance and predictable unit economics.
[00:08:48] Cam Nguyen: The cost savings from batching and caching were also material. But we did run a dashboard to make sure token accounting aligned with customer expectations — and Redwood's token-level breakdown helped.
[00:08:59] Alex Morgan: OK great. Let's do a quick recap and capture next steps. Sofia?
[00:09:05] Sofia Reyes: Recap: Redwood to prepare a draft case study and short podcast cut; Alex to send recording/transcript; Jordan to provide quote and headshot; Taylor to coordinate approvals. Timeline: transcript by 2/14, draft case study by 2/18, final approvals by 2/20.
[00:09:22] Jordan Lee: Sounds good. One small note — please redact any raw user PII from the transcript.
[00:09:27] Alex Morgan: Absolutely. We'll redact sensitive info before sharing publicly.
[00:09:31] Cam Nguyen: Quick technical follow-up — can you also share the benchmark spreadsheet you used when profiling us?
[00:09:36] Sofia Reyes: Yes, we'll attach the benchmark xlsx and the playbook.
[00:09:40] Taylor Brooks: I'll keep an eye out.
[00:09:43] Alex Morgan: Thanks everyone. Any final thoughts?
[00:09:46] Jordan Lee: No, thanks — excited to see the draft.
[00:09:49] Cam Nguyen: Thanks.
[00:09:51] Sofia Reyes: Thank you all.
[00:09:53] Alex Morgan: End recording.

[00:10:10] (Note: the rest of the meeting included off-record small talk and legal coordination that Taylor flagged for separate threads. Transcript truncated for brevity but original recording covers the 48-minute session with more detailed technical discussion and a short demo excerpt.)
